F-229: Gear ratio, so motors trade torque against top speed

Context
Raised 2026-08-12 by the tinkerer-audience design pass. A part's whole electrical story is one powerDraw number, which is a videogame stat rather than an engineering one. A per-axle gear ratio (torque up, top speed down) is a tradeoff mechanics already understand, costs one field on the connection, and makes wheel choice interesting for the first time.
Blocker (if any)
None. setDriveVelocity already takes a motor factor, so the plumbing exists.
Unblock condition
Ready: carry a ratio on axle connections, divide commanded velocity and multiply motor factor by it, and expose it in the workshop for axle mounts only. Bumps SIM_VERSION. Acceptance: a high-torque ratio measurably out-shoves a high-speed one and loses a straight-line race in unit tests, and the default ratio reproduces today's golden vectors byte for byte.
PR / Dot reference
Raised 2026-08-12 during the build-and-battle depth program.
Resolved
2026-08-12: shipped. Connection gained an optional gearRatio (0.5 to 2.5); AxleMotor carries it and the extracted pure gearedMotorCommand divides commanded shaft speed by the ratio and multiplies the motor factor by it, which is the torque-for-speed trade a reduction makes. Validity restricts a ratio to drive axles: a rigid mount has no motor and a spinner runs at a fixed velocity by contract, so a ratio on either would silently do nothing. Ratio 1 is the exact identity, proven by a test that runs the same 600-tick fight ungeared and at an explicit ratio 1 and asserts identical result hashes and combat state, so SIM_VERSION stays 5 and no stored replay was invalidated (same contract the B3 temperament slice used). Reduction costs power (GEAR_POWER_PER_RATIO 12 per axle per unit above 1, rounded to a tenth so float noise never reaches the budget or the UI), which makes torque compete with the weapon for the core's supply: the saw bot cannot afford maximum reduction, while a modest 1.2 still fits. Surfaced as a four-option Drive gearing panel that gears every drive axle at once and prices each option. Verified by 13 unit tests plus e2e E2E-WORKSHOP-0035. The behavioural half of the original acceptance (a tall gear losing a straight-line race) is NOT met and is recorded honestly as F-237: the bench showed the drivetrain is torque limited, so the commanded top speed rarely binds and reduction currently helps more than it costs at run time.

F-228: Weight classes and a pre-fight tech inspection

Context
Raised 2026-08-12 by the tinkerer-audience design pass. validateDesign already computes total mass and enforces a power budget, but mass is only a readout: nothing pushes back on it. Real weight classes give the budget something to press against, and framing validity as a tech inspection checklist (pass or fail per rule, in inspection language) turns an error list into the moment before a fight.
Blocker (if any)
None. Purely additive over the existing validation result.
Unblock condition
Ready: define classes by mass ceiling, let a design declare one, add the ceiling as a validity rule, and render the whole result as a checklist rather than a paragraph of errors. Acceptance: an over-weight design fails its declared class with a named rule, the class is enforced server-side at match resolve as well as in the workshop, and every existing stock design still passes in some class.
PR / Dot reference
Raised 2026-08-12 during the build-and-battle depth program.
Resolved
2026-08-12: shipped. New src/sim/weight-classes.ts defines four classes (Antweight 0.6, Beetleweight 0.9, Hobbyweight 1.4, Featherweight 2.2), sized against the shipped catalog so every stock archetype has a natural home and a unit test proves the rule never outlaws the shipped roster. BotDesign gained an optional weightClass, enforced inside validateDesign so the server rejects an over-weight bot at match resolve rather than trusting the workshop; undeclared designs stay unclassed and unconstrained, so everything that validated before still validates, and an unknown class id fails rather than passing silently. To present validity as an inspection without duplicating the rules, validateDesign now records a DesignIssueCode beside every message (errors is unchanged for existing callers) and inspectDesign groups those codes into seven checks: Parts, Core, Frame, Connections, Clearance, Power, Weight. Because the mapping is keyed by code rather than by matching error text, the checklist cannot drift from the validator, and a test pins that every check id is present. Surfaced as a Tech inspection panel with a per-rule pass or fail plus a weight-class picker (aria-pressed), replacing the flat error paragraph. The store setWeightClass is undoable and deletes the key when clearing, so a design round-trips to exactly what it was before classes existed. Verified by 14 unit tests and e2e E2E-WORKSHOP-0034. A duplication bug was caught in review of my own first draft: both validateDesign and inspectDesign appended the weight issue, so an over-weight design reported it twice; the inspection now only fills the gap when validation returned early on a structural fault before reaching the weight check.

F-227: Centre of mass, support polygon, and tip-over readout on the bench

Context
Raised 2026-08-12 by the tinkerer-audience design pass. The workshop shows part count, mass, and power, but not the numbers that actually decide whether a build works: where the mass sits, whether the wheels support it, and how far it can lean before it goes over. All three are computable from the placements computeLayout already produces, with no sim change at all.
Blocker (if any)
None. Pure geometry over existing data; the only cost is drawing it without allocating per frame.
Unblock condition
Ready: add pure helpers for centre of mass, the ground-contact support polygon from mobility parts, and the tip-over angle, then render a CoM marker and the support outline on the bench with a DOM readout for the exact numbers (Rule 10 keeps text out of the canvas). Acceptance: unit tests pin the CoM of a known asymmetric build, a nose-heavy build reports a worse tip-over angle than a balanced one, and the marker moves when a part is placed.
PR / Dot reference
Raised 2026-08-12 during the build-and-battle depth program.
Resolved
2026-08-12: shipped. src/lib/bot-balance.ts (lib, not src/sim: the tip-over angle needs Math.atan2, which the purity gate bans) computes mass-weighted centre of mass, the ground footprint, the stability margin, and the lean angle from the same computeLayout placements assembly uses. Contact points are modelled per shape: a horizontal cylinder rolling on its rim contributes a segment along its axis, a ball a point, anything else its footprint rectangle. The footprint threshold is SUPPORT_REACH 0.25 rather than a strict touching test, because a two-wheeled bot touches along a single axle line and a strict test reports it as having no fore-aft support and a tip-over of zero, which is alarming and useless; what the builder needs is how far it leans before the mass leaves the shape it can settle onto. Surfaced as a Balance panel in the Tune tab plus an opt-in bench overlay (centre-of-mass marker, plumb line, footprint outline) whose per-design geometry is disposed explicitly. The numbers reproduce the archetype intuition the cores exist to express: wedge 45.0 degrees, cube 40.4, tower 28.9. Verified by 13 unit tests (convex hull including the collinear and empty cases, signed hull distance inside/outside/degenerate, mass agreeing with validateDesign, symmetric bots centring, added mass moving the centre, the tall-versus-low ordering, nose weapons joining the footprint, design-order output, and an unresolvable design not throwing) plus e2e E2E-WORKSHOP-0033, which asserts the angle format, the aria-pressed state, and a real canvas pixel change when the overlay is switched on (Rule 10). Found and fixed a genuine bug while testing: the monotone-chain hull fell back to returning raw input on collinear points, which would have reported a bot balanced on one axle as having a real footprint.

F-226: Bench testing, so a build change can be measured instead of guessed

Context
Raised 2026-08-12 by the tinkerer-audience design pass, and the highest-value item in it. The sim is pure TypeScript and deterministic, so it can run far faster than the real-time arena, but the only way to evaluate a change today is to watch one 60-second fight. A batch runner that fights a design against a roster and reports win rate, median time-to-kill, and most-lost part turns building from taste into measurement. Pairing two designs closes the loop: change one wheel, see the win rate move.
Blocker (if any)
None. The cost is wall-clock: a full match is 3600 ticks, so a large batch needs either a worker or a capped roster.
Unblock condition
Ready: add a headless batch runner over resolveMatch that aggregates outcomes across the stock roster, and a workshop surface that reports the aggregate plus an A/B against a saved design. Acceptance: a batch is deterministic across runs, an obviously stronger build reports a higher win rate than an obviously weaker one, and the run does not block the main thread long enough to freeze the bench.
PR / Dot reference
Raised 2026-08-12 during the build-and-battle depth program.
Resolved
2026-08-12: shipped. src/sim/bench.ts adds BENCH_ROSTER (the three CPU archetypes plus the three replicas), runBench, and the pure compareBench. A roster pass resolves six full 60-second matches headlessly in about 1.2s (measured at roughly 196ms per match), so it is fast enough to run after every change. The report carries win rate, W/L/D, decisive wins versus timeouts, median time-to-kill over decisive wins only, average damage both ways, and a most-lost-part aggregate resolved to catalog names. Telemetry is enabled per bench match specifically so the report can name which parts were lost. Re-running after a build change reports the A/B: win-rate delta, damage deltas, per-opponent outcome flips, and which opponents were gained or lost. runBench takes an onMatch hook rather than calling a timer itself, so the sim stays free of host timers while the UI yields the main thread between matches. Surfaced as a Bench panel in the workshop Tune tab. Verified by 9 unit tests (roster integrity, tally consistency, determinism across two identical runs, progress ordering, part-name resolution, time-to-kill only counting disable wins, a real armed-versus-unarmed build difference being measurable, and two pure comparison cases) plus e2e E2E-WORKSHOP-0032, which runs two full roster passes in a real browser in 7.7s and asserts the headline percentage, one decided row per opponent, and the no-change A/B message. First finding from the tool itself: benching the starter Rammer shows five of six stock matchups running out the clock rather than reaching a disable, which is the stalemate F-232 and F-229 exist to address.

Context
Raised 2026-08-12 by the tinkerer-audience design pass. A fight ended with a banner naming the winner and nothing else. Per-part health, who hit what, when a part was lost, and which enemy part did it were all computed inside the sim and then thrown away, so a player could not act on a loss. This is the foundation the bench (F-226) and the replay overlay (F-233) both read from.
Blocker (if any)
None.
Unblock condition
Ready: record impacts and destructions as pure observation inside stepMatch, fold them into a per-part sheet, and render it after a test fight. Acceptance: recorded and unrecorded matches produce identical hashes, the logged damage reconciles with the combat scoreboard, and the sheet names the part that landed the killing blow.
PR / Dot reference
Raised 2026-08-12 during the build-and-battle depth program.
Resolved
2026-08-12: shipped. src/sim/telemetry.ts carries the rapier-free event types, the capped log (MAX_TELEMETRY_IMPACTS 4096, with impactCount staying honest past the cap), and the pure buildTeardown fold; createMatch takes an opt-in telemetry flag so the bench can still run unrecorded, and teardownInputFrom extracts the plain data the sheet needs. MatchTeardownSheet renders per-part damage bars, hits taken and dealt, the tick each part was lost, the enemy part that did the most damage to it, and the five hardest hits of the match. Determinism is proven two ways: the golden vectors did not move, and a unit test runs the same 600-tick fight recorded and unrecorded and asserts identical hashes, combat state strings, and end ticks. A second test reconciles the log against the scoreboard on a real 900-tick match. The live-match Playwright coverage is deliberately deferred to the bench slice: the stock test fight runs the full 3600 ticks and lands only 6 impacts, so an arena-driven e2e would be a 60-second test in an already timeout-stressed nightly, while the bench resolves a match headless in milliseconds and can hand the sheet a real teardown.

F-224: Prove the local gates actually pass on a Windows checkout

Context
Found 2026-08-04 while running the local gates from a Windows clone for the first time. The repository had no .gitattributes, so a Windows checkout applied core.autocrlf and converted every tracked file to CRLF. Three independent breakages followed, none of them visible from macOS, Linux, or CI. All nine scripts/*.sh failed under bash with $'\r': command not found, which takes out pnpm verify and the four check:* gates it wraps. Biome reported roughly 507 CR-only formatting errors across 508 files, because biome.json does not override the default lineEnding: "lf", burying the three real informational findings. And three suites failed to parse under Vitest with SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token: scripts/ci-functional-shards.test.mjs, scripts/ci-shadow-compare.test.mjs, and src/server/account-env-preflight.test.ts, which are exactly the three that import a scripts/*.mjs carrying a #!/usr/bin/env node shebang. The control case is ci-render-lib.test.mjs, whose import has no shebang and which passed. All three failed identically on main, so none of it was caused by the branch under test.
Blocker (if any)
None for the cause. The .gitattributes shipped with this entry pins * text=auto eol=lf, so every future checkout is LF on every platform. What is not yet proven is the effect. The fix was authored and validated on Linux, and the reporter's Windows host has not re-run the gates against a re-normalized working tree. The Vitest failure in particular has a diagnosed correlation but not a confirmed mechanism: node -e "import('./scripts/ci-shadow-compare.mjs')" printed parsed ok with the CRs still present, so Node parses those files fine and the fault sits somewhere in Vitest's transform rather than in the source. Removing CRLF should remove the trigger, but that is inference, not evidence.
Unblock condition
On a Windows host, take a fresh clone (or run git add --renormalize . against an existing one) and confirm four things: bash scripts/verify-local.sh --build completes instead of dying on $'\r'; pnpm lint reports only the three known informational suggestions rather than roughly 507 errors; the three named suites parse and pass; and git status stays clean, proving the renormalization matches what the repository already stores. If the three suites still fail with LF working files, the shebang correlation is not the whole story and this becomes a genuine Vitest transform investigation rather than a line-ending one. Also worth deciding then whether CI should gain a Windows job, since the reason this went unnoticed for the life of the repository is that every gate runs on Linux or macOS and nobody had run them from Windows.

F-205: Make the performance analyzer allocation-safe

Context
The analyzer measures the same GC pauses that froze real phones, but its own collection path creates steady garbage. The deep collector pushes a frame value into a growing array on every animation frame and replaces its frame, main-thread, network, and snapshot buffers each window. The compact sampler does the same with frame and draw-call arrays. PerfProbeBridge also creates then, catch, and finally callbacks inside useFrame each time it resolves GPU timestamps. These paths violate the frame-loop allocation rule and can distort the telemetry they collect.
Blocker (if any)
None. Lower priority than F-204 because the privacy boundary must fail closed first.
Unblock condition
Replace the deep and compact per-frame arrays with bounded, preallocated reusable numeric buffers and write cursors. Summarize only the populated prefix, reset cursors and window state in place, and keep upload queues strictly bounded without per-window replacement. Move GPU timestamp settlement to stable handlers or a non-frame scheduler so useFrame creates no Promise callbacks. Preserve all current percentile, draw-call, retry, partial-window, and source-transition semantics, including F-102's delivery contract. F-128: Define honest elevator journey telemetry

Context
The authoritative replay field elevatorRides counts successful rail action steps, including implicit entry and every auto-chained ride-up or ride-down segment. One player command can therefore count dozens or hundreds of rides on a deep shaft. Surface Down entry also increments the field and unlocks Ride the Rail even though the stamp says Ride the elevator from underground. Publishing the current field as adoption telemetry would mislabel implementation steps as player journeys.
Blocker (if any)
Resolve before using elevator usage in live product or economy decisions and before closing the placeable-elevator stamp review.
Unblock condition
Keep separate authoritative replay counters for rail action steps, implicit entries, total journeys, upward journeys, and downward journeys. A contiguous same-direction automatic sequence counts as one journey; surface or lateral entry plus its auto-chained descent also counts as one downward journey. Recommended default: Ride the Rail unlocks on the first successful journey in either direction and its copy becomes Take an elevator ride. If the underground-only copy stays, a surface descent must not unlock it. Add only the bounded counters to successful mine.cash_out balance events. Never retain coordinates, raw action logs, human error strings, or other high-cardinality dimensions. Tests must cover surface entry, lateral entry, deep auto-descent, upward return, direction reversal, interrupted travel, failed actions, and one journey from one player command.
PR / Dot reference
Dot VibeBots-f-128-define-fd4dbc01.
Monitoring update

A successful idempotent cash-out emits those deltas once, while a rejected or replayed submission emits no duplicate balance event. Keep lifetime achievement totals separate. Cover reload and retry of the same trip, two sequential trips, and a zero-journey cash-out so analytics can sum events without double counting.

PR / Dot reference
Dot VibeBots-f-127-stabilize-fee0d73b.
Monitoring update
The elevator feature branch full-suite run at commit 4178db62 produced a second failure shape in the same test: scene readiness and both horizontal movements completed, then Playwright ended the test while canvas.screenshot() waited for the before-strike frame. Diagnosis 2026-07-16
Reproduced and root-caused as a harness deadline false failure, not dropped input and not a product race. The historical CI trace (artifact 8301188352 from run 29308527889) was verified directly: on the retry, after ArrowRight the very next snapshot already read data-miner-x=1.00, data-miner-motion-frames=1, and data-horizontal-distance=1 (so on that trace the input and move had already succeeded before the failing poll result was delivered), but each Playwright round-trip ran 1-6 seconds because the retry captures a DOM snapshot per action (the dialog isVisible alone took ~6.6s; the initial getAttribute ended 112941.873, ArrowRight ran 112943.744 to 115558.172, the first poll getter after-event landed 117193.338 while the test-side expect.poll deadline expired at 117558.911 before the cross-process result was delivered). So the 1-2s polls on the ANIMATED data-miner-x expired before the matcher evaluated the already-correct value. Evidence supports the first attempt's Opening the shaft > 5s being the same round-trip-latency cause on the veil poll, and the raw second-shape artifact records locator.screenshot: Test ended. This trace proves the first ArrowRight succeeded before its poll result was delivered; it does not prove input always succeeds, that the startup shape shares the cause, or that snapshots explain every 1-6s latency. The screenshot shape was probed under a 10x CPU throttle: each canvas.screenshot() measured ~1.7-2.3s and the <canvas> bounding box settled by ~1.9s and never moved again, which supports cumulative-budget exhaustion (the 60s test deadline runs out during the last phase) without ruling out every intermittent raster or layout stall in the full shard.

Fixed harness-side only (no product change). The smoke mine actions begin immediately and settle smoothly (tests/e2e/mine-core.spec.ts) now proves each action through the authoritative, discrete data-horizontal-distance store signal on a budget that survives the per-op latency; it retains the data-miner-motion-frames > 0 smooth-motion proof (robust: a lateral retarget's creation frame sets frames to 1 before the rendered position reaches the target, and a direct snapMotion sets it to 0, so it still catches a teleport-instead-of-glide regression) and the rested data-miner-x position; and it adds a page-local keydown-to-store timing assertion (both stamps taken with performance.now() in the page) so a host-side budget still proves the action BEGAN immediately, measured in the browser and excluding Playwright's cross-process delivery. The load preamble waits on the authoritative data-scene-painted signal (the veil-release signal: the first painted frame, or the compile-gate fallback) and uses a load-tolerant locator assertion for the canvas position instead of a default-timeout async poll. Each phase is a test.step so a failure names the phase; the pixel-diff strike is kept unchanged. A CPU-throttled load stress smoke (tests/e2e/mine-core-throttled.spec.ts) exercises the acceptance-first path at 8x; it is honestly a stress smoke and not a red-green regression for the harness structure, because the CI failure is a trace-snapshot latency race that a CDP throttle on a fast machine did not reproduce (the old tight-poll structure still passed locally at 8x, 12x, and 16x, with and without trace). Resolved
PR #202 (branch fix/bunker-edit-revision-guard). Banked bunker edits now carry optimistic concurrency. The bunkers table gained a revision counter; loadBunkerView returns it and every state-changing write bumps it. The place, remove, move, and excavate wrappers take an expectedRevision and write through a guarded UPDATE (WHERE revision = expected, SET revision = revision + 1, RETURNING), so exactly one edit per revision wins; a stale expected revision, or a concurrent write that already won, returns HTTP 409 with the stable code bunker-revision-conflict and the authoritative view in the body. The dig CTE keeps the ore payout atomic with the guarded dug write and reports the dug row count so a lost race pays nothing. Reset, repair, and raid-start also bump the revision so an in-flight edit cannot clobber them. On the client, the store tracks the revision, echoes it as expectedRevision, and serializes every bunker write (the four banked edits plus buy, collect-loot, and skin) through one chain so a held-strike burst never overlaps and a non-bumping write can never carry a revision a concurrent edit already advanced past (each queued write reads the freshest revision); it drops any reply that would move the revision backwards, reports success only for a body it actually adopted, and on a conflict adopts the authoritative view (resync) then reports the edit as failed so a retry runs against fresh state. The conflict body is recognized by the shared bunker-revision-conflict code (moved to src/lib/api-codes.ts) rather than sniffing the body shape. Aim retargeting stays local and responsive; pending-claim edits stay on the synchronous local (mine-store) path, untouched. Older clients that omit the revision fall back to the loaded value, which still serializes concurrent writes through the guarded UPDATE. Covered by new server guard tests (match wins, stale rejects before writing, concurrent loss 409s, omitted-revision fallback, stale dig), a route test (revision threaded, 409 conflict body carries code and view), store scenario tests (serialized rapid edits thread the incrementing revision, out-of-order reply dropped, conflict resync then retry uses the fresh revision, duplicate same-cell dig fails without regressing, placement guarded too, collect-loot serialized behind an in-flight edit so its reply is not dropped), the full 1,464-test unit suite, and the banked first-person dig, place, and pry e2es asserting the expectedRevision in each request body. No player-facing surface changed, so no package bump, release note, tip, or stamp applies.

Post-merge correction (2026-07-16)
PR #234 merged as 0d8acac4. The prior Progress entry's statement that the third- and fourth-round atomicity and resurrection gaps were all addressed is superseded additively by exact-head review. The shipped resync deletes the caller slot's local trip before a typed authoritative snapshot exists, then lets loadWorld mutate live state before loadGear can fail. A server-selected active-slot change can replay an untouched local trip from another slot, and the moves-present gear path updates only top-level gear, leaving the mine or consumables stale. World and gear HTTP 200 bodies are not schema-validated, so missing fields can become plausible defaults and still authorize the later checkpoint clear. The clear accepts any successful status without requiring {cleared:true}, and its DELETE is unconditional by player id, so a late cleanup can erase a newer checkpoint PUT. The mutation success body is also untyped. A malformed 200, status-null transport loss, generic 503, or other ambiguous response can follow a committed write, but the client currently reports failure and leaves a blind retry available without reconciling the unknown outcome. Required acceptance: stage and validate world, pinned active slot, gear, full inventory, balance, checkpoint, and rail state before any local delete or live mutation, then commit the snapshot once; reject every malformed world, gear, and mutation 200; classify ambiguous transport as unknown and reconcile before controls re-enable; replace full inventory on accepted and rejected paths; clear a checkpoint only with a validated cleared:true body plus revision or fingerprint compare-and-delete and affected-row semantics; and keep a persistent blocking recovery surface with Retry plus Start fresh across reload until authority is restored. Tests must cover active-slot drift, world success plus gear failure, all malformed success boundaries, cleared:false, a newer PUT racing the late DELETE, lost-success transport, generic 503 after commit, no blind retry, complete state replacement, and recovery persistence.

Require every gear and consumable key, nonnegative integers within shared sim and database bounds, and equality between duplicated elevator, elevatorColumn, ladder, and plank values and their nested inventory values. Never independently accept gear and consumables, never normalize a partial object into defaults, and never fall back to local gear, bought stock, defaults, or rail-only fields. Any omission, extra or partial shape, numeric violation, duplicated-field mismatch, legacy body, active-slot drift, or movement away from the pinned surface snapshot performs zero local mutation or persistence and enters blocked reconciliation. Route tests must observe the real SQL projection rather than injecting inventory columns independently of the query.
Progress (2026-07-16, authoritative inventory)
The two headline inventory items are now DONE (branch fix/elevator-authoritative-inventory): adopting the full authoritative player inventory on a committed buy, and on an insufficient-balance reject. The route (/api/elevator/upgrade) now returns the full authoritative gear and consumables (the same shape /api/gear returns) on every accepted buy and every reject. The accepted-buy inventory is the EXACT committed row: both CTEs add the non-rail gear and consumable columns to their player_update ... RETURNING and project it with player_update.*, so the returned inventory is read inside the guarded write and is coherent with the balance and rail fields the same row returns (no follow-up SELECT that a later concurrent write could shift). Rejects carry the inventory from the pre-write profile (elevatorStateFromProfile) or the post-conflict re-read (reloadElevatorState, now selecting the full column set), spread through the shared ElevatorState bundle. A shared inventoryFromRow maps a row through the existing mineGearFromProfile/mineConsumablesFromProfile, whose parameter types were narrowed to MineGearRow/MineConsumablesRow Picks so a route reading only the inventory columns can map them. On the client (buyElevator), authoritativeInventoryFromResponse parses the response inventory as one atomic, strictly validated unit: every gear level a present integer at its floor and the column an integer or null (so normalizeGear cannot promote a garbage body to a level-1 snapshot), every consumable count a present non-negative integer, AND the duplicated top-level rail/support scalars must equal their nested values (same committed row). Any omission, malformed value, or mismatch yields null, and the client then adopts NOTHING from the inventory: the accepted path still applies the valid top-level rail scalars (the authority-critical rail depth, column, balance, trip index) and keeps last-known-good non-rail inventory, and a reject stays balance-only, so a partial or corrupt body cannot persist mixed rail authority. The non-rail staleness is reconciled by the server on the next fresh-trip gear load or the authoritative cash-out (a mid-trip loadGear refreshes only top-level gear, so it is not guaranteed on the immediate next load). This fallback is unreachable with the current server (which always returns a complete, valid, coherent inventory, proven by the route tests) and exists only for an older server that omits the objects or a corrupted response. When it validates, the accepted path adopts it wholesale (keeping the validated elevator depth and shaft column) before the usual surface-trip rebuild, and the insufficient-balance and rail-at-bottom rejects adopt it by rebuilding the surface trip over the UNCHANGED world (same base diff, replay the surface-only log) so gear/consumables stay in step with the live mine rather than a scalar merge that would desync it; the adopted rail depth equals the local one for both codes (else the classifier routes it through the full resyncCloudWorld refetch), so no rail desync is possible. A genuinely older server that omits the objects takes the same rail-only merge. A first exact-head review round asked for this strict/atomic/coherence validation plus tests that pin the CTE projection; those are addressed. Its broader demand to delete the compatibility fallback and enter a persistent blocked-reconciliation state on any invalid body (overlapping the separately claimed PR #236) was considered and NOT adopted: on a committed success the spend and rail extension already landed, so surfacing the valid authoritative rail and keeping self-healing last-known-good inventory is safer than blocking the UI, and the fallback preserves buys across a deploy skew; that stricter whole-response schema with a blocked-recovery state remains a possible future contract, tracked but not release-blocking for this item. Safe because buyElevator runs at the surface after banking any non-surface log, purchases sync to the server immediately, and the local bought buffer is always empty, so a wholesale adoption drops no locally-bought-unsynced stock. This returns the player only their own inventory to their own client, so it adds no telemetry surface. Still OPEN and NOT done (kept release-blocking): making expectedDepth required with a stable fail-fast 400 (a maintainer policy call, kept optional for backward compatibility); a persistent blocking recovery UI state (not just a reopen note) after a failed resync; a request id with durable, deduplicated structured mutation-outcome telemetry (outbox, exactly-once, fixed place/extend/relocate operations); the telemetry field-scrubbing pass; and an integration test exercising a real concurrent spend or bank race.

Progress (2026-07-16, blocking resync recovery UI)
The persistent blocking recovery UI is now DONE (branch fix/rail-resync-blocking-recovery). Before this, a rail buy that hit a conflict and then failed its authoritative refetch (offline mid-conflict) only set a dismissible shopNote ("couldn't refresh the rail; reopen the shop"), leaving the rail-buy control live over a known-stale local rail. The client now carries a distinct railResyncFailed flag (a gate on an action, not a transient note): the buyElevator conflict path sets it to !synced when resyncCloudWorld fails, and clears it on a successful refresh and on any accepted buy (both surface-only and post-bank success paths). A new retryRailResync store action re-runs the same bounded resyncCloudWorld; it clears the flag and notes success when the refresh lands, and keeps the block (re-noting the failure) when it fails again. It is a no-op when nothing is blocked, so it cannot fire a spurious refetch. In the elevator stall menu, while blocked the rail-buy button is disabled and a role="alert" recovery box appears with a native "Retry refresh" button (its own railRetryPending flag so the disabled buy button never mislabels as "Buying..." during a refresh; the two controls are mutually exclusive by railResyncFailed so no serialization is lost). One consistent rule (Rule 7): block only the rail-buy action, never trap the player (the shop still closes, mining continues), and the Retry affordance is always offered while blocked so recovery is self-healing when connectivity returns. Store tests cover the failed-refresh block, retry-success clear (world/gear/tripIndex adopted), retry-failure persistence, the no-op guard, and the accepted-buy clear; the stall-menu render test asserts the recovery box shows with an enabled retry and the buy control disabled while blocked, and neither appears in the normal state. The flag is scoped to the buy/retry flow that owns it (the only two resyncCloudWorld callers), not threaded into loadWorld; a rare peer-sync world reload that leaves the flag set is self-healed by one Retry tap against the already-fresh world. No new telemetry surface (client-only UI state, no shaft coordinates). Every outbox helper swallows its own errors: delivery retries and sink outages never fail or roll back a committed buy. Only committed (accepted) mutations get a durable row; rejects keep the existing best-effort log. F-120: Prevent reset-driven bunker ore farming and unsafe respawns

Context
Monitoring followup after PR #178. F-116 makes bunker rock yield normal ore, F-115 replaces the empty depth-zero plane with a pre-mined starter room, and F-119 keeps Reset accessible. The current reset contract clears every dug cell. Under the redesign, repeating Reset would recreate the same ore-bearing volume for unlimited rewards and would erase the starter room, leaving the next first-person spawn inside solid rock.
Blocker (if any)
Settle the reset contract before F-116 or the F-119 in-bunker Reset control ships.
Unblock condition
Reset must preserve server-owned resource depletion so no mined cell can pay out twice. Either keep excavation history or restore exhausted filler that yields no ore. Reset must always restore or preserve the F-115 starter pocket, choose a grounded passable spawn, retain the established active-raid guard, and settle the authoritative bunker plus player resources atomically. The Q-022 incompatible-layout path must fail fast with a clear Start fresh action and hard-reset old bunker state without migration or refund plumbing. Simulation, route, and end-to-end tests must repeat mine, reset, and reload cycles and prove total rewards do not increase, the pocket remains open, and the player never spawns inside rock.
PR / Dot reference
PR #180; Dot VibeBots-f-120-prevent-2b381d8f (child of VibeBots-first-person-3d-30115c4e).
Resolved
2026-07-14, across F-115 (package 0.1.256) and the F-116 ore economy (branch feat/bunker-ore-economy, package 0.1.261). The reset contract no longer clears the dug set: applyBunkerReset keeps bunker.dug (and the block seed) intact, clearing only the built parts and restoring core durability, so mined cells stay dug and cannot be re-excavated (isOpenBunkerCell rejects an already-open cell). With ore now real, this is what closes the farming vector: a dug cell credits ore exactly once (banked excavate credits on the dig; pending settles once at bank from the preserved dug set), and repeating Reset regenerates no ore because no cell re-solidifies. The starter pocket is preserved across reset and unioned on every load boundary (withSpawnPocket), so the first-person spawn is always grounded in an open room, never inside rock; the active-raid guard still blocks reset mid-raid, and truly incompatible legacy state hard-resets per Q-022. Ore payout, bag overflow, and the collectible-loot persistence share the server-authoritative bank and excavate transactions. Pinned by the reset unit tests (dug and pocket preserved) and the ore-economy unit and first-person e2e suites.
Post-merge correction 2026-07-14
The reset-preserves-dug rule and grounded pocket shipped, but the exactly-once and legacy-state claims above are not current truth. F-117: Rework bunker pieces into thin, rotatable, modular parts

Context
User request (2026-07-13 bunker redesign, item 4). Today each part fills a whole cell. Instead: floors are thin flat slabs the player walks over (not full blocks); walls are thin dividers on the boundary between two cells, rotatable, up to 4 per cell (one per horizontal face); floors may sit overhead when supported by at least two walls and are destroyed if a supporting wall is destroyed; roofs are thin like floors but only allowed on the top of the topmost cell; add rotatable modular staircase piece(s) for climbing between layers.
Design / recommended default
Shift the part model from cell-occupancy to sub-cell slot occupancy: a placed part records a cell plus a slot (floor, ceiling/roof, or one of four wall faces) plus orientation for stairs. Multiple parts can share a cell (up to 4 walls + a floor + a roof + a stair). Collision treats wall slabs as thin planes on cell faces and floor/roof slabs as thin planes at cell top/bottom; the DDA raycast targets the nearest slot face. Overhead floors need a support check (>=2 walls in the supporting ring); cascade-destroy dependent floors when supports break. Render-only thin geometry over the new thin colliders (part-visuals rule: colliders define shape). This is the largest change and likely bumps MINE_VERSION; existing bunkers are hard-reset rather than migrated (Q-022 resolved: only two alpha players, so reset existing bunker state instead of building refund or conversion plumbing).
Dependencies
Foundational for building; interacts with F-116 (what a "cell" is once it is a mineable block) and F-114 (place vs mine targeting). Sequence the slot model before or with F-116.
PR / Dot reference
(not started)

Q-022 is resolved: do not migrate, convert, or refund old full-block layouts. Fail fast with a clear incompatible-state response and a confirmed Start fresh action that hard-resets the old bunker before the thin-slot model loads.
Slice log
2026-07-15, branch feat/bunker-thin-parts-foundation, slice 1 of the arc (invisible groundwork, no package bump). Landed the sub-cell slot vocabulary in the pure sim as tested helpers, touching no mutation path: the BunkerSlot union (floor, roof, four wall faces, one interior mount), allowedBunkerSlots, isBunkerWallSlot, canonicalWallSlot with BunkerSlotRef (one divider per boundary), and an optional slot field on PlacedBasePart. placeBasePart, removeBasePart, and moveBasePart stay whole-cell, so the foundation never exposes a mutation API that could encode an unsupported floor or misplaced roof. Two new sim tests; the 25 existing bunker contract tests pass unchanged. Deferred to the slices that exercise them, sequenced so no persisted slot write precedes the version and reset boundary: slot-aware placement with its structural invariants (occupancy, overhead-floor support and cascade-destroy, roof-top-only and floor/roof plane co-location, exact-identity remove); then the persisted layout-version marker with the confirmed Start fresh reset and the destructive MINE_VERSION bump; then wire schema and persistence for slots, first-person raycast and thin geometry, the rotate control and stair part, and full-cell retirement. REQ-046 moved to partial.
Slice log
2026-07-15, branch feat/bunker-slot-placement, slice 2 of the arc (invisible sim, no package bump). Slot-aware placeBasePart/removeBasePart under the full structural invariants: canonical wall dedup, one part per slot, invalid-slot rejection, roof-top-only, and overhead-floor two-wall support with a grounded exception; prying a wall runs cascadeUnsupportedFloors to drop any floor that lost support (destroyed, unrefunded; pried wall still refunds). moveBasePart now ignores slotted parts so the cell mover cannot relocate one ambiguously. Floor/roof plane collision is prevented by construction (contradictory open/closed requirements on vertically adjacent cells). New exported cascadeUnsupportedFloors and BUNKER_OVERHEAD_FLOOR_MIN_WALLS. Nine new sim tests; the pre-existing bunker contract tests pass unchanged; full unit suite green (1529). The API is now complete enough that it cannot encode an invalid layout. Still no UI, persistence, or version/reset boundary (those remain the next slices). Slice log (review hardening)
2026-07-16, same branch, in response to an exact-head review of slice 2 before merge. Two corrections and five hardenings, all in the pure sim. (1) The roof rule was pinned by Q-025 to the dev direction "only the very top gets an actual roof": a roof is now allowed only in the volume's top row (footprint.row), not at any cell whose cell-above is closed; a mid-column room is capped with a second-story floor whose deck doubles as the lower room's ceiling. The earlier "top of the room" reading (slice-2 draft above) is superseded. (2) Structural settlement is now shared across every state change: excavating a cell runs cascadeUnsupportedFloors on the same path a pried wall uses, so digging the ground out from under a grounded floor drops it, and a wall chewed to zero durability no longer counts as floor support (so raid wear destroying the last live wall drops the floor above it). (3) A slot removal validates its origin cell is in the footprint before canonicalizing, so an out-of-bounds coordinate can no longer alias onto a real divider. (4) A bare-cell removal matches only a whole-cell legacy part, never a slotted one in a multi-part cell. (5) A whole-cell legacy part blocks a shared wall divider from either boundary order. Seven adversarial tests were added for exactly these cases (out-of-footprint origin, slotless removal in a multi-part cell, both boundary orders, zero-durability support, mid-row roof under rock rejected, raid-wear last-support drop, excavation under a grounded floor); the file now carries sixteen new slice-2 tests over the slice-1 baseline. Full unit suite green (1536). REQ-046 stays partial.
Slice log (review hardening, round 2)
2026-07-16, same branch, after a second exact-head review. This round corrects two overclaims from round 1 and closes three more gaps. Corrections: (a) the round-1 claim that "raid wear destroying the last live wall drops the floor above it" was overstated: the support count correctly ignores a zero-durability wall, but only a settlement pass (a pry or an excavation) actually drops the floor; nothing in live-raid wear settlement re-runs the cascade yet, so that integration is explicitly deferred to the raid-activation slice, and the test was renamed to describe what it proves (a pry cascade ignoring a rubble wall). (b) The round-1 interior-room test called a floor in the same cell "the lower room's ceiling", which is geometrically false (a floor slot is a cell's bottom plane); it is replaced by a test that digs two stacked cells, walls the lower one, and places the floor in the UPPER cell so its underside genuinely ceilings the room below. Hardenings: (1) legacy/thin-wall occupancy is now symmetric: a whole-cell legacy placement and a legacy move target are both rejected when a thin wall already divides one of the cell's boundaries (new bunkerCellBlockedByWall), so the physical boundary holds whichever part landed first, in both x and depth orders. (2) A slot removal now requires its origin cell to be open (excavated), not merely in the footprint, so a solid-rock or out-of-bounds coordinate cannot alias onto a divider through a cell the player is not in; covered for both the x and the depth (wall-nz) alias. (3) The server excavate write now persists parts atomically with dug under the same optimistic-concurrency guard, so a floor the dig cascades away cannot reappear on reload once slots persist (inert today because no slotted floor persists yet). Four new sim tests (second-story-floor ceiling, solid-rock depth-alias removal, legacy-on-thin-wall both axes, legacy move onto a walled boundary); twenty new slice-2 tests total over the slice-1 baseline. Full unit suite green (1540). Still deferred and tracked here: cascade integration into live-raid wear settlement, an unobstructed-shared-face check on authoritative excavation (a forged coordinate should not dig through a slotted wall or closed door), and dependent-mount (turret/spikes/stairs) settlement when a floor drops. REQ-046 stays partial.

2026-07-17, branch feat/bunker-slot-settlement, activation-blocker slice (invisible sim + wire, no package bump). Closed blocker 1, the last deferred activation blocker from the round-3 tracking record: live-raid wear now runs its settlement keyed on exact slot identity instead of the cell. Root cause was three identity keys built from cellKey(col,row,depth) that collapsed two thin walls sharing a cell into one entry: validateLiveRaidOutcome's snapshot map (which then rejected an honest two-wall report as part-wear because the map size dropped to one) and seen set, and settleLiveRaidOutcome's wearByCell map (which applied one durability to both walls). Fix: LiveRaidPart carries an optional slot (absent on legacy full-cell parts), createLiveRaid threads part.slot, and a new partKey(col,row,depth,slot) ("-" placeholder for the slotless legacy case, so legacy keys are byte-identical to the old cell key) replaces cellKey in both functions. The clanker nav (enterCost/livePartAt/stepOneClanker) is deliberately unchanged: it already tolerates multiple parts per cell by chewing standing parts one at a time via find(durability > 0), so a cell holding any thin wall stays blocked until every wall in it is gone. That is cell-granular defense (a wall protects its whole cell, not just its face) which is safe and deterministic; edge-precise nav (a wall blocking only the move across its own face) is a later raid-fidelity slice, not an activation blocker. The resolve route's partWear wire item gains an optional slot string (the snapshot identity match remains the real trust bound, matching the deliberately loose partId validation beside it). Five new sim tests (two walls in one cell validate distinctly, wear settles onto the exact slot not every part sharing the cell, an omitted wall and a duplicated slot each reject, a legacy no-slot part still validates and settles). tsc, Biome, dash clean; full sim suite green (404) and the server raid-live suite green (16). With blockers 1, 2, and 3 all landed, no activation blocker remains: the next slice may thread slot through the parts/bank wire and persistence (closing the Q-026 transient), then fp raycast slot targeting and thin geometry, the rotate control and stair part, and full-cell retirement. REQ-046 stays partial.

2026-07-18, branch feat/bunker-stair-climb, staircase climb movement (invisible pure modules, no package bump). Built the crux the plan flagged as highest-risk ("no precedent for a ramp in the discrete-cell mover"), and it turned out tractable. Design decision (user pick): asked how a staircase should move the player up a layer and the user chose the ramp model ("walk smoothly up") over the safer auto-jump step-up or a ladder-climb. So a staircase cell is a walkable ramp: crossing it in its ascent direction slopes the feet up one full layer. Implementation, all in the pure grid and movement modules (no canvas, no store): the grid gains four walkable stair values (FP_STAIR_PX/PZ/NX/NZ = 6-9) encoding the ascent direction, fpStairValue(orientation) and fpCellIsStair(value), and buildFpSolidGrid stamps a stair-panel part to the value for its orientation (the first real reader of the orientation field added in the data-model slice; fpCellBlocks stays false so a stair never blocks). The mover gains a per-frame ramp pass after the Y resolution: stairRampFloor finds the highest stair-ramp surface within FP_STAIR_REACH (0.55) of the feet in the capsule's column, and the step clamps the feet onto it (up while climbing, down while descending) leaving a jump off a stair intact. The ramp reaches full height over the first FP_STAIR_RUN (0.6) of the cell then holds a flat top landing, so the capsule tops out and clears an adjacent solid landing cell before its body would bump the landing's face (without the shelf the 0.3-radius capsule wedges at ~0.2 height, proven while building). A stairCeilingCap keeps the head from riding up into a solid ceiling cell, so a mis-built stair with no clearance blocks the climb instead of clipping through. All additions are scalar and allocation-free (frame-loop rule satisfied by construction; no canvas/render change, so the per-frame allocation profile is unchanged and the heap-churn A/B is not applicable to this pure-module slice). Still invisible: the stair stays comingSoon, so no stair part exists in production and the ramp code never fires yet; it activates when placement ships. Tests: 6 movement tests (climb one layer up the facing direction, slope height on the incline, walk back down, ceiling blocks the climb without clipping, orientation reverses the slope, a plain floor is unaffected) and a grid test (the four values map to orientation, are walkable, and buildFpSolidGrid stamps a stair by orientation with a legacy no-orientation stair defaulting to +x). tsc, Biome, dash clean; full unit suite green (1720). REQ-046 stays partial. Remaining: staircase placement (fp full-depth stair geometry, the orientation/rotate control, the place-route + orientation persistence wire) and the reveal (drop comingSoon, grant starter inventory, release chain); then full-cell retirement (which closes Q-026).

In first person a sealing part (wall, floor, roof, door) is now placeable only on a matching sub-cell slot: placeOk in bunker-fp-canvas.tsx gained a placement.valid term, so aiming a wall at a floor or roof face (which yields no slot) is rejected outright, hiding the ghost and the place cell, instead of dropping in a legacy whole-cell block. Context

Generate the claim volume's rock from the mine's own cell generator keyed to the claim's world depth, so bunker blocks carry the same kinds, ore, and hit counts. F-115: Spawn into a pre-mined 3x2x2 bunker room

Context
User request (2026-07-13 bunker redesign, item 2). A fresh claim currently opens the whole 7x5x1 tunnel plane, which reads as a flat wall rather than a room. Instead, pre-excavate a small 3x2x2 pocket around the spawn so the player clearly stands inside a room, with solid mineable rock all around to dig outward.
Design / recommended default
At claim time, seed the dug set (or its successor) with a 3-wide by 2-tall by 2-deep pocket centered on the spawn cell instead of opening the full depth-0 plane; everything else starts solid. The spawn stays grounded on the pocket floor facing into diggable rock. Small once F-116's generation model is in place; can ship a first version over today's excavation model with a fixed pocket.

Context

Design / recommended default
Add a first-person pickaxe view-model with a swing animation triggered per strike (allocation-free, driven from the existing rig useFrame). Hold-to-mine: while the act input is held and the crosshair rests on a diggable cell, auto-repeat the dig at the block's break cadence with a cracking-progress overlay that resets when the target changes. Drag retarget: the mined cell always follows the current crosshair/held target, so dragging look (touch) or moving the mouse (desktop) mid-hold moves the strike to the newly targeted in-range cell. Reuse FP_MAX_REACH. Per RULE 10, prove the swing and crack move with consecutive-frame pixel diffs.
Dependencies
The "striking a real block" payoff pairs with F-116 (real blocks with break counts and ore), but the swing/hold/drag interaction can land first over the current single-tap dig.

F-112: Validate pending bunker checkpoints and offer recovery

Context
The account trip route accepts pendingBunker as unknown data, the client only checks that parts is an array, and the normalizer dereferences every element. A malformed checkpoint such as parts: [null] can therefore throw instead of producing a stable state error. The checkpoint path has also accumulated validation in multiple layers.
Blocker (if any)
none; this is current-state cleanup and is ready now.
Unblock condition
Define one shared bounded pending-bunker schema and normalizer for the route, client, and persistence layers. Invalid cells, core data, part entries, dimensions, and excessive collection sizes must return a stable incompatible-state response without replacing the last known good local state. Show a clear Start fresh trip recovery action, and cover null parts, malformed core data, bad dug cells, oversized arrays, and supported legacy shapes.
PR / Dot reference
Dot VibeBots-f-112-validate-81ed1e44 (child of VibeBots-first-person-3d-30115c4e).
Resolved
PR #204 (branch fix/pending-bunker-validation). One bounded Zod schema, pendingBunkerBuildSchema in src/server/mine-trip-schema.ts, now guards the pending-bunker checkpoint for all three layers: the account trip route (pendingBunker went from z.unknown() to the schema, so a malformed checkpoint is rejected with a stable 400 before any storage write), the client trip-response reader (accountTripFromResponse), and local persistence (loadLocalTrip). The scattered shallow guard isPendingBunkerBuild and the hand-rolled normalizePendingBunker that dereferenced part.depth on a null element (the throw) are gone; normalizePendingBunker now delegates to the schema and returns null on invalid input instead of throwing. Structural corruption (a null or non-object part, a non-object or partial core, a malformed or missing-depth dug cell, an oversized parts or dug collection, an out-of-bounds footprint) rejects the whole checkpoint as a stable incompatible-state; legacy shapes still coerce (a missing or out-of-range part/core depth clamps onto the tunnel plane, a missing dug list is empty, and the spawn pocket is re-seeded via withSpawnPocket). A present-but-invalid stored checkpoint is dropped rather than resumed half-broken, and the last known good in-memory state is never replaced: loadLocalTrip returns null and removes only the unusable blob. The recovery action is a clear auto-fresh-start scoped to genuine corruption: a new storedTripPendingBunkerIsCorrupt predicate lets the local resume path show Your saved trip couldn't be restored, so a fresh one started. only when a checkpoint's pending bunker fails validation, while a routine version or shape mismatch keeps resetting silently as it always has (Rule 7: auto-recover with a notice beats blocking on a manual button). Two review refinements keep valid trips safe: an unrecognized cosmetic skin id (a trip from a newer build) coerces to the default rather than rejecting the whole trip, and the checkpoint's part-durability bounds match the authoritative bank route (min 1, max 1000) so a checkpoint can never resume locally yet be rejected at bank. Covered by new persistence unit tests (null part does not throw, non-array parts, malformed core, bad dug cell, oversized parts array, null pending passthrough, valid pending seeds the pocket, a stored malformed checkpoint is dropped, a stored valid checkpoint still loads, a version mismatch is not flagged as corruption, an unknown skin coerces to the default), a route test (a malformed pending bunker is rejected 400 with no storage write), and a store test (the fresh-start notice surfaces and the unusable blob is cleared) on top of the existing legacy-depth-normalization coverage; full 1,477-test unit suite green, typecheck and production build clean. The bank route keeps its own flat claim schema (a different wire shape, authoritative and separately tested); it is intentionally not folded into this checkpoint schema. No player-facing feature changed (the incidental fresh-start notice is a safety message, not a mechanic), so no package bump, release note, tip, or stamp applies.
Post-merge correction (2026-07-15, PRs #204 and #205)
The shared schema removed the original null-part throw, but the recovery and bounds acceptance remains open. Corrupt local state is deleted automatically before the player can choose, and the notice says a fresh trip already started. Replace that with a fail-fast incompatible-state view that preserves the bad blob and last known good state until the player confirms Start fresh trip. Tighten the single schema so it rejects arbitrary smaller footprints, cells outside the footprint, duplicate cells, claim coordinates that disagree with the footprint, unbounded record keys and blockSeed, and unknown skinsOwned values that currently normalize to undefined. Cover each hostile shape, cancellation of recovery, one confirmed reset, reload before and after reset, and no partial replacement. Preserve the historical Resolved entry and closed Dot as evidence of the narrower slice; active successor Dot VibeBots-finish-f-112-c8429f3b owns the remaining acceptance.
Preservation boundary correction (2026-07-15, PR #223 full review)
Until the player confirms Start fresh trip, preserve both the malformed checkpoint blob and the last known-good local state. Detection, cancellation, navigation, and reload must not delete or replace either one, start a clean trip, or partially adopt data from the bad blob. Reload presents the same incompatibility choice. One confirmed reset removes the malformed blob exactly once, starts one clean state, and keeps that clean state on the next reload. Cover cancellation, reload before confirmation, confirmation, duplicate confirmation, reload after confirmation, and no deletion or partial replacement before the boundary.

F-110: Bound live raid upload and resolver work

Context
A live raid trace turns a short defense event into a user-controlled request and deterministic pathfinding workload. Without explicit limits, an oversized or numerically hostile trace can consume excessive request memory, replay time, or concurrent resolver capacity.
Blocker (if any)
The trace shape and authored raid durations must be fixed by F-104.
Unblock condition
Cap request bytes, ticks from server-authored duration plus grace, coordinate ranges, enemies, pathfinding expansions, and simultaneous resolves per player. Reject non-finite values and impossible array shapes before simulation, keep the core protected from partial writes, and return stable validation codes for every rejected limit. Add boundary and adversarial route tests plus a worst-case resolver budget test.
PR / Dot reference
Dot VibeBots-f-110-bound-d2131ab6 (child of VibeBots-first-person-3d-30115c4e).
Rescope (2026-07-15, Q-024)
Largely descoped. The upload-bounding half disappears with the player trace: there is no user-controlled trace body to cap for bytes, ticks, coordinate ranges, or array shape, so those adversarial-input limits and the worst-case-trace resolver budget test are dropped. What remains is trivial and folds into F-108's snapshot work: the resolver runs a server-authored, fixed-length wave over a bounded 7x5x5 volume, so a single sanity assertion that tick count stays within the authored duration plus grace and that pathfinding expansions are naturally bounded by the finite grid is enough. The single-resolve concurrency guard that this item also mentioned stays, but it belongs to F-106 (conflict/resync), not here.
Rescope corrected (2026-07-15, Q-024 option D)
Supersedes the note above. Under option D the client reports a raid outcome to the server, so there IS a request body to bound, just a small one, not a full trace. Keep a slim version of this item: cap the reported-outcome payload size, reject non-finite or impossible values, require the reported damage and rewards to fall within what the frozen start snapshot allows, and settle exactly once. Drop the oversized-trace, tick-cap, and worst-case-pathfinding-budget concerns, since the server does not run the pathfinding.
Progress (2026-07-15)
The pure bounds primitives landed in src/sim/bunker-raid-live.ts: LiveRaidOutcomeReport (the small verdict/attrition/XP/part-wear payload a client sends), liveRaidOutcomeReport to derive it from a settled raid, and validateLiveRaidOutcome(snapshot, tier, report) which proves the report is internally consistent and no better than the frozen snapshot and wave allow (version, loss-is-a-death, tick within duration plus grace, kills within the wave, no reward on loss, reward capped by the wave's total XP, and each worn part maps to a distinct snapshot part with durability only ever reduced), returning a stable rejection reason. Twelve unit tests cover the happy path and each rejection. Still pending for the server slice: the HTTP request byte cap and the exactly-once settle guard, which belong to the resolve route (with F-106).
Monitoring correction (2026-07-15, PRs #209 and #215)
liveRaidOutcomeReport currently converts an active state into a win, so a tick-zero report with no death, no kills, unchanged wear, and zero XP can pass validation. Report derivation and server validation must require a real terminal state: every Clanker is dead or the authored duration has actually elapsed. Bind report.raidId to the selected row, enforce the current raid version and expiry in the same guarded settlement, and retain a hard request-byte limit before parsing. Cover tick zero, one tick before timeout, the exact timeout boundary, all-enemies-dead, an active report marked survived, a stale raid id, unsupported version, and a post-expiry resolve.
Production exploit evidence (2026-07-15, PR #221)
Main c84a4403 accepts a tick-zero win, does not bind the submitted raid ID to the selected newest row, does not reject a past-grace resolve, and permits client-reported defense XP and kill counts without terminal or cross-field consistency. Settlement then grants survival vibes, XP, and stamps. The route parses JSON before a hard byte cap. Require one guarded validation boundary for identity, supported version, server expiry, terminal state, killed-to-XP consistency, bounded server-derived telemetry, and request bytes. Cover a stale report settling a newer raid, a late win racing expiry, claimed maximum XP at zero kills, and no reward or progress for every rejection.
Thin-slot report-bound correction (2026-07-19)
The resolve route caps partWear at 200 from the earlier 175-cell model, but thin modular slots let one banked cell retain several tracked parts and incremental placement does not impose a 200-part bunker total. validateLiveRaidOutcome requires exactly one wear entry for every tracked snapshot blocker and floor spike, so an honest dense bunker can exceed the route schema before the validator runs. PR / Dot reference
Dot VibeBots-f-109-pin-6a12d11e (child of VibeBots-first-person-3d-30115c4e).
Progress (2026-07-15)
Sealed semantics for the live model landed in src/sim/bunker-raid-live.ts: the raid tracks a breached flag that flips the first time any Clanker enters the footprint, and liveRaidSealed(state) is a survive with no breach (nothing ever got in). It is exposed on LiveRaidOutcomeReport.sealed and the validator rejects a sealed flag on a loss (a breach happened by definition), while a sealed win is trusted since it only gates the cosmetic Buttoned Up stamp. Monitoring update (2026-07-15, live-test telemetry)
The only new live lifecycle signal is the success-only bunker.live_raid_reward balance event. Add one bounded server-derived outcome event for accepted and rejected start, resolve, expiry, and incompatible-state recovery so live testing has a loss and failure denominator. Use fixed operation, result, and reason values; omit coordinates, raw reports, wear arrays, snapshots, seeds, and human text. Keep the reward balance event success-only and exactly once, document it in the README alongside bunker.raid_reward, and prove a telemetry sink failure cannot fail, roll back, or duplicate gameplay settlement.
Zero-durability projection correction (2026-07-15)
The live sim can chew a defense to zero and settlement persists that zero-durability part, but first-person render and collision currently treat every persisted part as intact and solid. Define zero durability as a nonblocking destroyed state that can remain server-owned for repair without looking or colliding like a healthy defense. Project the transition at the sim action tick, preserve it through settle and reload, and restore the healthy render and collider only after authoritative repair. Cover wall, door, spike, reload, repair, and Clanker plus player traversal through the same opening.
Production telemetry correction (2026-07-15, PR #221)
The deployed bunker.live_raid_reward event includes a unique raid ID and client-reported kill count even though the count is only range-bounded and can disagree with XP or terminal state. Remove the raid ID and untrusted tuning field. Keep the success-only balance event server-derived, bounded, and exactly once. Add one separate fixed-reason lifecycle event covering accepted and rejected start, resolve, loss, expiry, conflict, incompatible-state recovery, retry, and sink failure, with no report, wear, snapshot, coordinate, seed, or human-text payload.
Forfeit telemetry review (2026-07-15)
The draft on-demand forfeit emits no lifecycle event, so live testing cannot distinguish an accepted abandonment from no active row, stale version, concurrent resolve, duplicate request, or persistence failure. Route it through the bounded server-derived lifecycle contract with fixed operation, result, and reason values, no raid ID or payload, exactly one event for each accepted or rejected request, and non-fatal sink failure. Do not emit the success-only reward balance event for a forfeit.
Telemetry idempotency contract (2026-07-15, PR #223 review)
Use the shared tuple (operation_family, logical_request_id, event_kind) as the internal event key. The logical request ID is the authoritative settlement or mutation identity when one exists; otherwise the request must carry a bounded idempotency token. Persist the request-to-result mapping and uniquely keyed outbox row atomically with the gameplay transition, or with the fixed rejection record when no transition commits. A retry looks up the same tuple, returns the recorded result, and never enqueues a second event. Keep the tuple out of analytics fields; pass it only as a sink idempotency token or deduplicate delivery durably. If the sink cannot deduplicate a crash after send but before acknowledgement, describe delivery as at least once instead of claiming exactly once. Cover duplicate requests, retry before and after commit, rejection, crash after send, sink failure and recovery, conflict, expiry, and no-op. F-150 uses the same tuple and replay rule for payout and balance events.
Merged telemetry scope rejection (2026-07-15, PR #224)
Comment 4980856802 dismissed raid lifecycle telemetry as out of scope, then PR #224 merged as main 98d269ee with no telemetry change. The existing F-109 contract separately owns bounded start, resolve, loss, expiry, conflict, recovery, rejection, retry, and sink-failure outcomes. F-101 maps the user's new in-base telemetry request to the missing bounded performance context. Both production gates remain open.
Fallback-token context binding (2026-07-15, PR #223 exact review)
Bind every fallback server-scoped idempotency token to the actor, operation family, event kind, canonical digest of the server-relevant lifecycle inputs, bounded expiry, and recorded outcome or conflict state. Store the digest instead of raw sensitive payload. Validate every binding before returning a request-to-result mapping. An unexpired identical context replays the stored result and emits no second event; cross-actor reuse, the same token with different inputs, conflicting state, or expired reuse returns a stable rejection and cannot return another actor's result or suppress a legitimate lifecycle operation under a fresh token. Cover each case. F-150 shares this binding and replay rule.
Exactly-once scope correction (2026-07-15, PR #223 full review)
The older exactly once phrases apply only to the committed gameplay transition or fixed rejection result and the uniquely keyed outbox enqueue. One logical request creates at most one recorded result and one outbox row, and a replay returns that result without another transition or enqueue. Sink delivery is at least once unless the sink deduplicates the stable internal key. Never claim exactly-once network delivery across a crash after send and before acknowledgement. Cover one transition and enqueue, replay, retry before and after commit, duplicate delivery, sink deduplication, and the non-deduplicating crash window. F-150 keeps the same delivery boundary.
Out-of-band sink-health correction (2026-07-15, PR #223 full review)
Do not report a lifecycle sink failure through the same failed sink. Persist bounded delivery attempt state on the uniquely keyed outbox row and emit one fixed-reason telemetry_sink_failed health record through the independent server monitoring logger or an equivalent health channel. Include only operation family, event kind, attempt state, and a fixed error class. Omit actor, request, raid, report, snapshot, and human text. Never enqueue the health record into the lifecycle sink, never create another lifecycle outbox row for it, and swallow health-channel failure so recursion or gameplay impact is impossible. Cover sink outage, retry, recovery, terminal failure, health-channel failure, no recursive record, and unchanged gameplay settlement.

Live testing still cannot distinguish accepted forfeit from no active row, unsupported version, conflict, concurrent resolve, duplicate request, network failure, or sink failure. Keep F-109 open. Record accepted and rejected outcomes under the existing fixed-value, privacy-bounded, idempotent request-result and outbox contract, with no reward event for forfeit and independent non-recursive sink-health reporting.

Every older phrase that lists sink failure among lifecycle or touch-abandon outcomes is historical and superseded for request-result semantics. One logical forfeit request records at most one accepted or rejected gameplay result and one uniquely keyed lifecycle outbox row. A lifecycle sink outage never becomes a gameplay result reason, never creates an additional request-result or lifecycle outbox row, and never changes the replayed result. Persist delivery-attempt state on the existing outbox row and report at most one bounded telemetry_sink_failed delivery-health record through the independent non-recursive monitoring channel defined above.
